name: Ziryab depilatories

card.summary: Chemical hair-removal products said to have been introduced for women in 9th-century Al-Andalus by the court trendsetter Ziryab, for a smooth, groomed look.
card.note: The attribution is poorly sourced; historical depilatories could be caustic.

quick.overview:
Ziryab was a 9th-century musician and tastemaker at the court of Cordoba in Al-Andalus, credited in later accounts with spreading many grooming habits. Wikipedia's hair-removal article says chemical depilatories for women were introduced in 9th-century Al-Andalus by him, though it marks the claim as uncited.

The appeal was smooth, hair-free skin without shaving. The Ziryab article itself does not mention depilatories, only shaving, haircuts, a deodorant and an early toothpaste.
quick.how: Details of the products are not recorded in the accounts consulted. Depilatories in general are creams or pastes applied and wiped off.
quick.risks: Chemical depilatories can burn or irritate skin, and ancient formulas sometimes included harsh or toxic ingredients such as orpiment (arsenic trisulfide) in lime pastes used historically elsewhere.

lead: Ziryab (9th century) is remembered as a trendsetter at the Umayyad court in Al-Andalus, credited with popularising face shaving, new short haircuts with straight bangs, a deodorant, an early toothpaste, and twice-daily bathing.[2] Many of these claims are hedged ("said to", "thought to") and the article carries an accuracy-dispute tag; much of the material traces to a Saudi Aramco World article by Robert Lebling.[2]

Separately, the hair-removal article states that chemical depilatories for women were introduced in 9th-century Al-Andalus by Ziryab, noting that this claim lacks a citation.[1] The Ziryab article does not mention depilatories.[2]

angle.text: The attribution concerns women's hair removal for smooth skin; specifics of the products are not documented.

paras: The claim appears in a general history of hair removal, which also covers ancient Greek and Roman depilatories, Egyptian depilation and the slaked lime, ash and orpiment paste used since antiquity.[1]

Ziryab is credited with shaving among men, the straight-fringe haircut leaving ears and neck free, and replacing rose-water hair washing with salt and fragrant oils.[2] The claim that he opened beauty parlours for elite women is not supported by early sources.[2]

timeline.event: Chemical depilatories for women said to be introduced in Al-Andalus by Ziryab.[1]
